questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: Vaccines were once assumed to work through a single, uniform mechanism: introducing a weakened or partial pathogen so the immune system could recognise and neutralise the real version later. Immunologists studying antibody response over the following decades complicated this assumption considerably: some vaccines generate a strong initial antibody response that fades within months, while others generate a comparatively modest initial response that nonetheless produces memory cells capable of mounting a rapid defence years later, meaning the size of the immediate antibody response and the vaccine's actual long-term protection turn out to be only loosely related, a distinction that has reshaped how researchers now evaluate a new vaccine's effectiveness.

options.text: Why Every Vaccine Works Through an Identical Immune Mechanism
Why Immediate Antibody Response and Long-Term Protection Are Only Loosely Related
A History of Vaccine Development in the Twentieth Century
Why Antibody Levels Always Predict a Vaccine's Long-Term Effectiveness
How Researchers Manufacture Weakened Pathogens for Vaccines

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A hospital that increases the intake of patients eligible for an organ transplant programme is often assumed to be straightforwardly expanding access to care. Health policy researchers studying actual outcomes complicate this assumption: a larger intake without a corresponding increase in available donor organs simply lengthens the average waiting list, meaning some patients who would previously have received a transplant within a viable window instead deteriorate while waiting, an outcome the expanded intake was never designed to allocate for. Hospitals that instead pair intake expansion with active donor recruitment report genuinely improved outcomes, suggesting the intake figure alone says little about whether access has actually improved.

options.text: the surgical procedures involved in organ transplantation
how expanding transplant programme intake without more donors can worsen outcomes rather than improve access
the total number of organ transplants performed annually worldwide
why hospitals rarely publish their transplant waiting list data
a comparison of two specific hospitals' transplant programmes

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A prosecutor deciding whether to pursue a case built substantially on circumstantial evidence faces a genuine strategic dilemma: pursuing a weak case that ultimately fails can damage the prosecutor's credibility for future cases, while declining to pursue a case that might have succeeded lets a genuinely guilty defendant escape conviction entirely. Prosecutors who consistently decline any case lacking overwhelming direct evidence maintain impressive conviction rates but are sometimes accused of allowing guilty defendants to go free simply to protect that statistic, a tension that has led some jurisdictions to evaluate prosecutors on case outcomes relative to case difficulty rather than on raw conviction rate alone.

options.text: the legal standards required for circumstantial evidence to be admissible
how evaluating prosecutors by raw conviction rate can create an incentive to avoid genuinely difficult cases
the total number of circumstantial-evidence cases prosecuted annually
why defendants prefer circumstantial evidence over direct evidence
a comparison of two specific jurisdictions' prosecution rates

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: An army's battlefield success is often attributed almost entirely to troop numbers and equipment quality, factors that are visible, easily counted, and satisfying to compare between opposing forces. Military historians studying prolonged campaigns complicate this attribution considerably: a numerically and technologically superior army that cannot sustain its own supply lines over an extended campaign frequently loses to a smaller, better-supplied force, suggesting that logistics, an unglamorous factor rarely emphasised in popular military history, determines outcomes at least as often as the troop numbers and equipment that dominate most retellings.

options.text: Troop numbers and equipment quality alone always determine battlefield success.
Logistics may determine battlefield outcomes at least as often as the more visible factors typically emphasised.
Military historians agree that logistics has no measurable effect on campaign outcomes.
A numerically superior army always wins regardless of its supply situation.
Popular military history always accurately emphasises the true causes of victory.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
I spent a full year assuming my elderly neighbour simply preferred to be left alone, since she never once accepted my early, occasional offers to check in on her. It wasn't until her nephew mentioned, almost in passing, that she had actually been hoping someone would ask more than once, that I understood declining a single offer had never meant declining help altogether, only that she felt awkward accepting help the very first time it was mentioned. I started simply checking in on her every Sunday without asking first, and within a month she was the one initiating conversation, asking me in for tea before I'd even knocked properly. I still feel a flicker of regret that it took her nephew's comment, rather than my own persistence, to notice what I had been missing.

Statements
(a) The writer initially assumed her elderly neighbour preferred to be left entirely alone.
(b) The neighbour had accepted the writer's early offers to check in on her.
(c) The nephew suggested the neighbour had actually been hoping someone would ask more than once.
(d) The writer began simply checking in every Sunday without asking first.
(e) The neighbour eventually began initiating conversation herself.
(f) The writer credits her own persistence, rather than the nephew's comment, for noticing the misunderstanding.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Military historians studying recruitment posters from major conflicts have proposed two competing explanations for why appeals to abstract national duty gradually gave way to appeals emphasising concrete personal benefit, such as guaranteed trade training. One explanation holds that public enthusiasm for a given conflict predictably declines the longer it continues, and recruiters simply adapted their appeal to whatever motivation remained most persuasive as abstract patriotic sentiment faded over time. A second, competing explanation instead proposes that recruiters had access to increasingly sophisticated audience research throughout the period, and the shift reflects better data about what actually motivated potential recruits rather than any decline in patriotic sentiment among the public at all.

options.text: The first explanation attributes the shift to declining public enthusiasm for a given conflict over time.
The first explanation suggests recruiters adapted their appeal as patriotic sentiment faded.
The second explanation claims patriotic sentiment among the public actually increased throughout the period.
The second explanation attributes the shift to increasingly sophisticated audience research.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same shift from abstract duty to concrete personal benefit.

questions.text: Which of the following questions CANNOT be answered from the passage?
questions.context: Specialised military corps, distinct units organised around a single function such as engineering or medical support rather than general combat, emerged gradually as armies grew too large for a single generalist force to manage every logistical need efficiently. Military historians studying this specialisation note that armies which developed dedicated engineering corps early gained a measurable advantage in besieging fortified positions, since purpose-trained engineers could construct siege works far faster than general infantry attempting the same task without specialised training. This advantage, however, came with a corresponding cost: maintaining multiple specialised corps required a far more complex supply and command structure than a single generalist force, a cost some smaller armies could not sustain despite recognising the tactical benefit clearly.
